chapters.title: Chapter 5: Matching the Method to the Business

lessons.title: Sum-of-the-Parts Valuation for Conglomerates and Holding Companies

children.text: Some Indian companies cannot be valued with a single method, because they are not a single business. A group may run a cement plant, a specialty chemicals unit, a lending arm and hold a large stake in a listed consumer company. Applying one P/E or one EV/EBITDA multiple to the consolidated numbers treats all of that as one thing, which it is not. The answer is to value each part with the method that fits it, then assemble the pieces.

body.text: Value each part on its own terms, then account for what the parent adds or subtracts: corporate costs, parent-level debt, taxes on unlocking value, and the discount investors apply to holding structures.

children.text: When Sum-of-the-Parts Is the Right Tool
Diversified conglomerates with segments in unrelated industries.
Holding companies whose main assets are stakes in other listed companies.
Manufacturers with a captive lending arm, such as an auto company with an NBFC subsidiary.
Groups with large non-core assets: land banks, treasury portfolios, stakes in associates.
Companies about to demerge a division, where the market is repricing the parts.

body.text: Start with the segment disclosures in the annual report. Indian companies report segment revenue, results, assets and liabilities under Ind AS 108, which gives you the building blocks. Quarterly results usually carry a shorter version of the same table.

cells: Identify segments and separate holdings from segment disclosures
Segments that mix very different businesses; unallocated items
Use the method that fits: DCF, EV/EBITDA, P/B, market value for listed stakes
Mixing enterprise values and equity values in the same column
Surplus land, treasury investments, stakes in associates
Valuing land at book cost rather than realistic value net of tax
Parent net debt, unallocated corporate costs, minority interests
Forgetting that corporate overheads are a permanent drag on value
A holding company discount where shareholders do not control the underlying cash flows
Applying a discount twice, or ignoring it entirely

body.caption: Matching the method to each part

cells: Consumer or IT businesses with steady cash flows
P/B against ROE, or residual income
Multiple of its own earnings or book, or a DCF
Market value net of tax and selling costs

body.text: The most common sum-of-the-parts error is mixing enterprise values with equity values. An EV/EBITDA multiple gives the value of a business before debt; a P/B multiple for a lending arm gives value after its borrowings. Add them up carelessly and you will subtract the parent's debt from a total that already excludes some of it. Keep a separate column for each and label every line.

children.text: Bharatvarsha Industries Ltd is a fictional NSE-listed group with 60 crore shares trading at ₹250. It runs a cement business, a specialty chemicals business and a non-banking finance subsidiary. It also owns 32.0% of a listed FMCG company with a market capitalisation of ₹18,750 crore, holds surplus land worth ₹800 crore net of tax, spends ₹150 crore a year on head office costs that are not charged to any segment, and carries ₹3,500 crore of net debt at the parent level, excluding the finance subsidiary's borrowings.

cells: Net asset value before holding discount
Less: 20.0% discount on the listed stake
No control over the investee's cash flows

stats.label: Market price

children.text: Two things stand out. First, the cement and chemicals businesses together are worth ₹15,000 crore, but head office costs and parent debt remove ₹4,625 crore of that before any of it reaches shareholders. Corporate costs are not a rounding item: capitalised, they are worth as much as a small business. Second, the value is spread across four very different assets, so a single consolidated multiple would have told you nothing useful.

body.text: Tax matters when value is unlocked. If Bharatvarsha sold its listed stake, worth ₹6,000 crore against a cost of ₹900 crore, long-term capital gains tax at 12.5% would take roughly ₹638 crore, leaving about ₹5,363 crore. This is part of why holding structures trade below the market value of what they own: shareholders cannot access the full amount.

children.text: routinely trade far below the market value of the stakes they own, often at discounts of 40% to 70%. The discount is not irrational, and understanding what drives it is the whole job.

markDefs.definition: Companies whose principal assets are shareholdings in other companies, often within the same promoter group, rather than an operating business of their own.

body.title: What widens and narrows a holding company discount

columns.label: Widens the discount
points: No control over the underlying companies' dividends or strategy
Tax leakage if stakes are ever sold
Head office costs with no offsetting business
Low free float and thin trading volumes
Promoter groups with no intention of unlocking value

columns.label: Narrows the discount
points: A credible plan to demerge or list a division
Buybacks or higher dividends that pass value through
Stakes in businesses that pay generous dividends
An operating business of its own that funds the holding costs
Activist or institutional pressure for change

children.text: Several large Indian groups have reorganised in recent years, spinning off financial services arms and other divisions into separately listed companies. When such an event is announced, the discount usually narrows, because shareholders can finally own the parts directly. Bajaj Holdings and Tata Investment Corporation are long-standing examples of listed Indian holding companies whose market values have historically sat well below the value of their holdings.

body.label: The practical question with any holding company
body.value: Is there a catalyst, or is this permanent?
body.context: A 60% discount that has persisted for a decade with no change in structure is not necessarily an opportunity. It is the market pricing a permanent arrangement. Look for a specific, dated reason the discount should narrow.

body.caption: Common errors and how to avoid them

cells: Debt is subtracted twice, or not at all
Label each line as enterprise or equity value and reconcile at the end
Counting a subsidiary's profits inside consolidated earnings and its stake value separately
Value the subsidiary once, and exclude its contribution from the parent's numbers
Counting dividend income and stake value
Dividends from a stake are included in the parent's cash flows while the stake is also valued separately
Exclude dividend income from investees when valuing the stake at market value
Full value of a partly owned subsidiary is credited to shareholders
Deduct the share owned by others, as in the Chapter 3 bridge
Head office costs are treated as if they disappear
Capitalise unallocated costs after tax and deduct them
Lending arm debt is added to parent debt and subtracted again
Value the lender on equity value; leave its borrowings inside that valuation

body.title: Assemble the parts
body.prompt: A group's manufacturing segments are worth ₹5,000 crore on an enterprise value basis. It owns a listed stake worth ₹2,000 crore. Parent net debt is ₹1,500 crore. There are 25 crore shares and no corporate cost adjustment or holding discount. What is the sum-of-the-parts value per share, in ₹?
body.explanation: Equity value = ₹5,000 crore (enterprise value of operations) - ₹1,500 crore net debt + ₹2,000 crore stake = ₹5,500 crore. Per share = ₹5,500 ÷ 25 crore = ₹220. Note that the stake is already an equity value, so no debt is subtracted from it.

body.title: Discount to NAV
body.prompt: A listed holding company's stakes are worth ₹500 per share at market value. Its shares trade at ₹180. What is the discount to net asset value, in %?
body.explanation: Discount = 1 - (₹180 ÷ ₹500) = 64.0%. Discounts of this size are common among Indian holding companies. The question is whether anything will change that, such as a demerger, buyback or higher dividend payout.

body.title: Spot the double count
body.question: An analyst values a conglomerate by applying an EV/EBITDA multiple to consolidated EBITDA, which includes its 60% owned subsidiary, and then adds the market value of that subsidiary's listed shares. What is wrong?
options: The subsidiary is counted twice: once inside consolidated EBITDA and again as a separate stake, and the 40% owned by others is not deducted
EV/EBITDA should never be used for conglomerates
The subsidiary should be valued on P/E instead
body.explanation: Consolidated EBITDA already includes 100% of the subsidiary. Adding the market value of the stake counts it a second time, and the minority shareholders' 40% must also be deducted. Either exclude the subsidiary from consolidated figures and value it separately, or keep it inside and subtract non-controlling interest.

body.title: Why the gap exists
body.textWithBlank: Indian holding companies typically trade at a large ___ to the market value of the stakes they own.
body.explanation: The discount reflects lack of control, tax on unlocking value, holding costs, low liquidity and, often, no expectation of change.

body.title: The 65% discount that never closes
body.scenario: Aman, an investor in Ludhiana, finds a listed holding company whose only assets are stakes in three listed group companies, worth ₹9,000 crore in total at market prices. Its own market capitalisation is ₹3,150 crore, a 65% discount. It has no operating business, receives about ₹120 crore a year in dividends from the stakes, spends ₹35 crore on corporate costs, and pays out ₹40 crore as dividends. The promoter family holds 75% of the company and has never sold a share. The structure has been the same for 15 years, and the discount has ranged between 55% and 70% throughout.
body.prompt: Is this an opportunity? What would have to change for the discount to narrow?
body.modelAnswer:
1. The discount is not new information. It has persisted between 55% and 70% for 15 years, so the market has priced this structure consistently. Buying simply because the discount exists is a bet that a decade and a half of pricing is wrong.
2. Cash flow to shareholders is small. Of ₹120 crore of dividends received, ₹35 crore goes on corporate costs and only ₹40 crore is paid out. On a ₹3,150 crore market capitalisation, that is a dividend yield of about 1.3%. Shareholders receive very little of the underlying value each year.
3. There is no control and no catalyst. With the promoter family holding 75% and never selling, no activist can force change and no takeover is possible.
4. Tax would reduce any unlocking. Selling the stakes would trigger capital gains tax, so the realisable value is below ₹9,000 crore.
5. What would change it: a formal demerger or amalgamation that gives shareholders direct ownership, a large buyback, a sharply higher dividend payout policy, a promoter decision to simplify the group, or the sale of one stake with proceeds distributed.

How to act: treat the holding company as a slow compounder that tracks the underlying stakes, plus a small dividend, rather than as a discount that will close. If Aman likes the underlying businesses, he could compare owning them directly. Only if a specific, credible catalyst appears does the discount itself become the investment case.

body.title: Build a sum-of-the-parts from an annual report
steps: Open the segment information note and list every reportable segment with its revenue and results.
Decide the right method for each segment, and note whether it produces enterprise value or equity value.
Find the investments note and list stakes in listed and unlisted companies, with holding percentages.
Value listed stakes at current market prices; value unlisted stakes on their own fundamentals.
List non-core assets such as surplus land and treasury investments, and value them net of tax.
Find unallocated corporate costs in the segment note and capitalise them after tax.
Take parent-level net debt from the standalone balance sheet, and keep any lending subsidiary's borrowings inside its own equity valuation.
Deduct non-controlling interests for partly owned subsidiaries.
Decide on a holding discount, justify it, and state the catalyst that could narrow it.

points: Use sum-of-the-parts when a group's segments have different economics, risks and valuation methods.
Value each part with the method that fits it, and keep enterprise values and equity values in separate columns.
Deduct parent net debt, capitalised corporate costs and non-controlling interests before reaching equity value.
Value listed stakes at market prices, and remember the tax that would be payable if they were ever sold.
Indian holding companies often trade 40% to 70% below net asset value, for reasons including lack of control, tax and holding costs.
A persistent discount is only an opportunity if there is a specific catalyst, such as a demerger, buyback or higher payout.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Bharatvarsha Industries Ltd, the holding company described and the individuals named are fictional, and all figures are illustrative. References to Bajaj Holdings and Tata Investment Corporation describe long-observed market characteristics and are not recommendations. Tax rates change; confirm current rules with a chartered accountant. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before making investment decisions.
